The proposed merge rule fails. On the even grid, take three types with admissible sets \(A=\{2,4\}\), \(B=\{4,6\}\), and \(C=\{2,6\}\). The first two sets are single even-grid intervals, and the third is a union of two singleton intervals. Each pair has a witness: \(A\cap B=\{4\}\), \(B\cap C=\{6\}\), and \(C\cap A=\{2\}\). Yet \(A\cap B\cap C=\varnothing\), so every choice the receiver could make fails for at least one type.

Three types are minimal when each type has at least one admissible witness. One such type is feasible by itself, and for two types the pairwise check already supplies a common witness. If empty admissible sets are permitted, a singleton group containing such a type fails vacuously and can be rejected at the outset.

**Exact criterion.** A nonempty label group \(G\) is feasible exactly when \(\bigcap_{t\in G}S_t\ne\varnothing\), where \(S_t\) contains all witnesses admitted by type \(t\) across its alternative methods. Necessity follows because the receiver takes one action for the label, so its witness must belong to every \(S_t\). Conversely, the receiver can use any witness in the intersection. Different types may admit that witness through different methods.

I used the note’s single-interval observation to look for a gap in one type’s admissible set.

The draft should retain both states in the loss calculation. Each state admits a successful setting, but the worker receives the same information in both states and must choose once. Either deterministic choice therefore succeeds in one state and fails in the other. Ordinary work can be credited with realized recovery if the chosen setting matches the realized state. It cannot be credited with guaranteed recovery across both states.

Let \(p\) be the probability of choosing \(k=1\). Since the state is indistinguishable at decision time, the same \(p\) applies in both states. The success probabilities are \(1-p\) when \(z=0\) and \(p\) when \(z=1\). Their minimum is at most their average, \(1/2\). A fair coin attains \(1/2\) in each state, so the sharp worst-state success probability is **\(1/2\)**. This calculation needs no prior on the states.

For the appendix, let \(I(z)\) denote the information available when acting and \(S(z)\) the set of feasible settings that achieve recovery in state \(z\). Attribute guaranteed recovery to a substitute exactly when there is an implementable rule \(g\) such that \(g(I(z))\in S(z)\) for every relevant state. Thus, for each possible observation, the rule must select a setting in the intersection of the success sets of all states consistent with that observation. Here the intersection is \(\{0\}\cap\{1\}=\varnothing\).

I used the note’s statement that a successful configuration exists separately for each state. The workbook reference was unnecessary for the argument.

Replace the draft sentence with this criterion. **One binary message suffices exactly when the following graph is bipartite.** Its vertices are the sender’s types. Join two types \(u,v\) if some desk \(y\) allows both and \(I(u,y)\cap I(v,y)=\varnothing\).

For a counterexample, take three types \(A,B,C\) and three desks, named \(AB,BC,CA\). At each desk, give the first named type the interval \(\{2\}\), the second named type \(\{4\}\), and the remaining type the interval \(\{2,4\}\). These are intervals in the positive even integers. The same two witnesses \(2,4\) pierce every desk’s intervals. Yet desk \(AB\) forces \(A\) and \(B\) to send different labels, desk \(BC\) forces \(B\) and \(C\) to differ, and desk \(CA\) forces \(C\) and \(A\) to differ. Two labels cannot meet all three requirements.

To prove the criterion, any successful encoding must give distinct labels to adjacent types. Otherwise the receiver at the desk defining that edge would have to choose one witness in two disjoint intervals. Thus the two labels give a proper two-coloring.

Conversely, fix a proper two-coloring and let each type send its color. For any desk and received color, the compatible types of that color have pairwise intersecting intervals. If the family is nonempty, let \(b\) be its smallest right endpoint. Every interval meets an interval ending at \(b\), so its left endpoint is at most \(b\). Its right endpoint is at least \(b\) by definition. Hence every interval contains \(b\), which the receiver can choose. An empty family corresponds to a desk and color that cannot occur together.

I used the note’s fixed-label observation and its suggestion to test a short cycle.

Replace the draft sentence with: **Two message values suffice exactly when the following graph is bipartite.** Its vertices are the sender’s types. Join two types \(u,v\) if some desk \(y\) admits both and \(I(u,y)\cap I(v,y)=\varnothing\).

For a counterexample to the draft, take three types \(a,b,c\) and three desks admitting, respectively, the ordered pairs \((a,b),(b,c),(c,a)\). At each desk give the first type interval \(\{2\}\) and the second interval \(\{4\}\). The witnesses 2 and 4 pierce every desk’s intervals. But each listed pair must send different messages: at its shared desk, the receiver must distinguish the two singleton intervals. This would require three pairwise different messages.

To prove the replacement, any valid sender rule using two message values gives a two-coloring. Adjacent types must receive different colors because their shared desk cannot answer a common message with a witness in both disjoint intervals.

Conversely, fix a proper two-coloring and have each type send its color. For a given desk and received color, the compatible types of that color have pairwise intersecting intervals. If there is at least one such interval, let \(r\) be the smallest of their right endpoints. Every interval meets an interval ending at \(r\), so its left endpoint is at most \(r\). Its right endpoint is at least \(r\) by construction. Thus \(r\) is a positive even witness acceptable to every compatible type. Desk–color combinations with no compatible type never occur.

I used the note’s observation that a sender who knows the desk can choose a desk-specific message. Here the same coloring must work across all desks.

The proposed merge rule fails, even when every type has an admissible witness. Take three types with witness sets \(A=\{2,4\}\), \(B=\{4,6\}\), and \(C=\{2,6\}\). The first two are single intervals on the even grid. The third is the union of two singleton intervals. The pairwise intersections are \(A\cap B=\{4\}\), \(A\cap C=\{2\}\), and \(B\cap C=\{6\}\). Since \(4\notin C\), no witness serves all three types.

Three types are minimal among types with nonempty witness sets. One type can use any of its witnesses, and for two types the pairwise check already tests the entire intersection. If empty witness sets are allowed, a singleton group containing such a type also fails, since the pairwise check is vacuous.

**Exact merge criterion.** A label group \(G\) is feasible if and only if \(\bigcap_{t\in G} S_t\neq\varnothing\), where \(S_t\) contains all witnesses admissible for type \(t\), across its permitted methods. Necessity follows because the receiver chooses one witness for the label, which must serve every type in the group. Conversely, any witness in the intersection supplies a valid receiver action. Thus the editor can retain all scientific substitutes for each type and intersect the resulting sets across types.

I used the note’s suggestion to test whether different pairs could share different witnesses.

Ordinary work can recover the missed direction in either state, but the draft cannot credit both states as recovered. The receiver sees the same message in both. A receiver who sets \(k=0\) succeeds in state 0 and fails in state 1. Setting \(k=1\) reverses the outcomes. Either fixed setting therefore has worst-state success probability zero. In a realized case, recovery can be credited if the setting actually used matched the state.

For a randomized rule, let \(p\) be the probability of setting \(k=1\). The receiver has the same information in both states, so the same \(p\) applies in both. The success probabilities are \(1-p\) in state 0 and \(p\) in state 1. Their minimum is at most \(1/2\), since they sum to one. A fair coin attains \(1/2\) in each state, so the sharp worst-state success probability is **\(1/2\)**. This calculation requires no prior over states.

For guaranteed substitution, let \(I(z)\) denote the information available when acting and \(S(z)\) the settings that meet the scientific need in state \(z\). Credit guaranteed recovery exactly when there is one admissible rule \(g\) such that \(g(I(z))\in S(z)\) for every state under consideration. In this example the common message would require a setting in \(S(0)\cap S(1)=\{0\}\cap\{1\}=\varnothing\). The draft establishes only that each set is individually nonempty, which does not justify dropping either state from the loss calculation in advance.

I used the note’s suggestion to fix one receiver rule and evaluate it in both states.
